\subsection{Counting collapses at a finite $k^\ast$}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) shows counting accuracy against $k$. Every model
reproduces the shape the theorem predicts: accuracy is high for small $k$, then
falls to a floor and stays there. Pooled over the panel, accuracy is
\AccRepLow{}\% at $k\le3$ and \AccRepHigh{}\% at $k\ge6$. Past the collapse point
the errors are not random: at $k\ge8$, \LoopPct{}\% of generations run long
(looping or overcounting) and \TruncPct{}\% stop short --- precisely the two
behaviours available to a decoder whose stop decision has lost access to the
count.

The collapse point $k^\ast$ ranges from \kStarMin{} to \kStarMax{}
(Table~\ref{tab:models}). Within the Qwen3-TTS family it doubles from $0.6$B to
$1.7$B, so scale buys a longer horizon --- but a bounded one, exactly as
\eqref{eq:horizon} says it should. The effect is not specific to repeated single
words: repeating a whole \emph{sentence} produces the same curve, and number
phrases with intrinsic digit-word repetition (\emph{six hundred sixty-six
thousand six hundred sixty-six}) fail at the modest counts their structure
imposes. The unit can be a word, a phrase, or a place-value pattern; what matters
is that it recurs.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(b) is the paper's sharpest test. Each control item has the
same carrier sentence and the same word count as its repeated twin, and differs
only in that the $k$ copies of one word are replaced by $k$ distinct words. If
the failure were about sequence length, attention span, or accumulated exposure
bias, the two curves would coincide. They do not: at $k\ge6$, repeated items are
rendered correctly \AccRepHigh{}\% of the time against \AccCtlHigh{}\% for
controls. Models that cannot say \emph{very} six times in a row will say twelve
or sixteen \emph{different} adverbs without difficulty.

One alternative deserves ruling out: repeated text is unusual text, so perhaps
models fail on it because it is improbable rather than because it is periodic.
That would require the controls to be the more natural member of each pair. They
are not. Scored under a general-purpose causal LM, the control is the \emph{less}
probable member in \NllCtlHigherPct{}\% of the \NllPairs{} matched pairs (mean
per-token NLL \NllCtl{} vs.\ \NllRep{}), and the gap widens monotonically with
$k$. The harder-to-predict text is the one models render correctly, so
naturalness runs opposite to the effect.

\subsection{The states the decoder visits stop multiplying}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says that under periodic conditioning the states a
decoder visits stop being mutually distinguishable. The observable consequence is
that asking for more repetitions should stop buying the decoder more distinct
internal states, while the same amount of non-repetitive text should keep buying
them. We measure the number of distinguishable states as the effective rank
$\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \exp(-\sum_i p_i \log p_i)$ of the generation
trajectory over normalised singular values, and the statistic is the
\emph{capacity gain} $\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$,
with intervals bootstrapped over stimulus templates.

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(c,d) shows the result. On repeated text the capacity gain
is a factor \CapRatio{} of the control gain, with disjoint 95\% intervals for
\NCapSepWord{} of the \NCapModels{} instrumented checkpoints; the matched-pair
form of the comparison gives a positive gap in \CapFracPos{}\% of pairs. The
decoder does not merely make mistakes on repeated text --- it runs out of
internal states in which a mistake and a correct continuation could differ.

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} is checkable in the same recordings, and it concerns the
softmax \emph{restricted to the $k$ repeated keys}: raw attention weight is
normalised over the whole sequence, whose length itself grows with $k$, so it
confounds dilution with sequence growth. Renormalised over the occurrence
columns, the profile entropy grows with $\log k$ at slope
\BlockEntropySlope{}, the implied spread is $\delta \le 0.06$ nats across the
whole ladder, and no occurrence --- not even the most attended --- ever captures
more than $1.9/k$ of the block's mass. Attention over the repeated spans is
within a few percent of uniform, which is what Assumption~\ref{ass:periodic}
needs. The trajectories also reproduce the spectral signature the companion ASR
study reported under stress: reduced effective rank and hardened spectra in
hallucinated generations. Per-model tables are in the supplement.

\subsection{Two things we could not establish}
\label{sec:negative}

We first tried to estimate $q$ directly, locating each repetition boundary from
the model's text attention and fitting
$\log\lVert h_{m+1}-h_m\rVert = a + m\log q$. That estimator is unsound here:
boundary localisation needs a monotone text read-head, and the deep-layer
attention centroid of these decoders advances on barely half of generation steps,
so boundary estimates collapse onto near-duplicate positions and the distances
measure localisation error rather than state dynamics. The failure is
self-defeating by construction --- the flatter the attention over repeated spans,
exactly what Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution} predicts, the worse any attention-based
localiser gets. The capacity measure needs no boundaries, which is why we adopted
it.

Second, we cannot claim the count is \emph{absent} from the states. A ridge probe
trained to recover $\log_2 k$ from trajectory summaries, cross-validated across
carrier templates, decodes it only coarsely, and better from non-repetitive text
than from repeated text --- consistent with degradation, not erasure. Since a
linear probe is exactly the readout class Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(iii)
constrains, a stronger probe recovering the count would matter; we could not rule
that out at this panel size.
